html:
I’ll talk about giving talks in English.

I’m one of the slow ones: when I first went abroad, I had never given a talk in English. Before my first talk I memorized almost everything I was going to say, and once I had it down pat, I varied the linking words a little and added some pauses so it wouldn’t sound so recited. After a few talks I had a routine and grew fluent, and then I could stop memorizing and just prepare the key words and sentences.

For anything that’s hard to say, heavy on logic or hard to explain, practice it several times until it rolls off your tongue. This goes especially for the introduction or background, which many people tend to treat lightly, putting all the emphasis on their own “hardcore” material. But if the audience doesn’t understand what your work is actually good for, who’s going to listen for the next ten, twenty or more minutes? In the third year of my PhD I had some results and had made a breakthrough as a speaker too, and then at a conference someone asked me straight out: what is this actually useful for? It drained my battery on the spot. In fact, explaining your project clearly in one or two sentences is very hard. Say too much and people have long since drifted off. This is what’s known as the elevator pitch: you happen to meet an investor in the elevator, and selling yourself in the shortest possible time before the elevator arrives is a real art. After thinking about it for a long time, and experimenting on people outside my field, I finally distilled two or three sentences that sum up my project.

I suggest putting some thought into working a little humor into the opening. It grabs everyone’s attention and relaxes the room, and when you see someone in the audience laugh, you relax too. Also, don’t talk too fast: nobody knows your project as well as you do, and no one else can keep up with your train of thought. Slowing down also helps you organize your thoughts and think on your feet, so you don’t tie yourself in knots.

Finally, put in plenty of time and practice. Nobody steps on stage and speaks brilliantly from the start, least of all PhD students new to the field. You may point out that professors can get up and hold forth without any preparation, but that’s decades of accumulated experience; they started out just like us. In the later part of my PhD I stopped respecting talks: I barely prepared, just went up and talked, and thought I was pretty damn good. After a few of those I realized there was a lot I had meant to say and hadn’t, and the bits that could have shone fell flat. Only at my PhD defense did I take it seriously again. I prepared for several days and rehearsed about twenty times, until I could talk about any slide at the drop of a hat. A defense talk is bound to be more nerve-racking than usual, but because I was well prepared, once I got through the nerves of the first few minutes I grew smoother and more confident as I went. It went very well, and I consider it the best talk I gave in my whole PhD. So until you become a big shot, take the time to prepare properly, and practice in front of the mirror a lot.
